AC9M7N03: Write 60 405 as a sum using powers of ten.
What is the value of the digit 7 in 47 206?
A student writes 5 032 = 5 × 10³ + 3 × 10² + 2. Correct the error.
The 3 is in the tens place: 5 × 10³ + 3 × 10¹ + 2 × 10⁰.
Why does 10⁰ appear in the units term for a nonzero ones digit?
10⁰ = 1, so multiplying by 10⁰ gives the number of ones.
Compare 4 × 10³ + 9 × 10¹ and 4 × 10³ + 9 × 10². Which is larger and by how much?
A place-value chart has 2 hundred-thousands, 0 ten-thousands, 6 thousands, 0 hundreds, 3 tens and 4 ones. Write the numeral and explain the two zeros.
206 034. The zeros hold the ten-thousands and hundreds places; omitting them would change the other digits' places.
Write the natural number 90 008 in expanded notation. Check by adding the terms.
AC9M7N04: Write 3/5 as a decimal and percentage.
For example, 8/14 and 12/21; multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number.
A student writes 2/3 = 3/4 by adding 1 to both numbers. Disprove the claim.
2/3 = 8/12 but 3/4 = 9/12. Equal additive changes do not preserve the ratio.
A number line from 0 to 1 is divided into eight equal intervals. Name the point five intervals to the right of zero in fraction and decimal form.
Which is closer to zero: -0.4 or -3/5? Explain using a number line.
-0.4 is closer. Its distance from zero is 0.4, compared with 0.6.
Order 0.35, 1/3 and 34% without treating their written forms as different kinds of quantity.
Write a rational number between -0.3 and -0.2 in fraction and decimal forms.
For example, -1/4 = -0.25. Other correct numbers in the interval are acceptable.
AC9M7N05: A calculator gives $27.486 for a final price. State the price to the nearest cent.
Why might rounding every intermediate result give a different final answer from rounding only at the end?
Small rounding errors can accumulate. Keep extra precision during the calculation.
A 12.6 m rope is cut into 2 m lengths. How many complete lengths can be made? Explain why ordinary rounding is inappropriate.
6 complete lengths. Rounding 6.3 up would claim more full lengths than the rope provides.
A bus holds 40 people. How many buses are needed for 93 people? Explain the rounding decision.
3 buses. 93/40 = 2.325, but two buses cannot carry everyone.
A student reports 3.2 × 9.8 = 313.6. Use an estimate to judge the result, then calculate correctly.
The estimate 3 × 10 = 30 shows 313.6 is too large. The correct product is 31.36.
AC9M7N06: Calculate 2.4 × 0.5 and explain the size of the answer.
1.2. Multiplication by one half halves the quantity.
A 2.5 L jug contains 1.75 L. How much more liquid is needed to fill it?
A recipe needs 3/4 cup of oats for one batch. How many cups are needed for 2 1/2 batches?
A student adds 1/2 + 1/4 and gets 2/6. Explain and repair the method.
The parts have different sizes. Use quarters: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.
An $80 item is reduced by 15%. Find the discount and the sale price, then check the total.
AC9M7ST02: For 4, 6, 6, 8, 11, find mean, median, mode and range.
Make a stem-and-leaf plot for 12, 14, 17, 21, 21, 26. Include a key.
Stem 1: leaves 2, 4, 7. Stem 2: leaves 1, 1, 6. Key: 1 | 2 means 12.
A data set is 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. Which value is unusually large, and which average is most affected?
18 is unusually large compared with the cluster; the mean is affected more than the median.
Two groups are A: 4, 5, 6 and B: 1, 5, 9. Compare their means and ranges.
Both means are 5. A has range 2; B has range 8, so B is more spread out.
8, the mean of the two middle values 7 and 9.
Add 30 to the set 5, 6, 7. Compare the old and new mean and median.
Old mean and median 6. New mean 12; new median 6.5. The mean changes much more.
Why should a report about a distribution describe spread as well as centre?
Sets can have the same centre but very different variation, as in the two groups above.
Use graphing software or squared paper to draw a dot plot for 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 4. Describe its cluster and range.
Two dots at 1, three at 2 and one at 4. Most values cluster at 1–2; range 3.
AC9M8N01: Estimate √45 to one decimal place. Explain why it lies between 6 and 7.
Write the exact circumference of a circle of diameter 12 cm, then approximate to one decimal place.
Explain why √36 is rational but √37 is irrational.
√36 = 6. Since 37 is not a perfect-square integer, √37 is irrational.
π ≈ 3.14. The finite decimal is an approximation, not the exact irrational value.
A square has area 50 cm². State its exact side length and a two-decimal approximation.
Locate √10 between two consecutive tenths without using a rounded square-root display.
A circular garden has radius 2.8 m. Find its exact area and round to one decimal place.
A student says a calculator's finite display proves √2 is rational. Explain the limitation.
The display has limited digits and shows an approximation. It does not show the infinite non-terminating, non-recurring decimal expansion.
AC9M8N02: 3⁷; add exponents when multiplying powers of the same base.
Evaluate 12⁰ using a quotient of equal powers to explain why.
Simplify (5²)³. Explain why the exponents multiply.
5⁶. Three factors of 5² contain six factors of 5 altogether.
Compare 2³ + 2³ with 2³ × 2³. Why do they use different methods?
The sum is 16; the product is 64. The multiplication law does not apply to addition.
Write three expressions equal to 10⁶ using a product, quotient and power of a power.
Is 3² × 4² equal to 12²? Justify from repeated multiplication.
AC9M8N03: Convert 3/8 to a decimal and classify it.
Explain why a calculator showing 0.16666667 has not shown the exact value of 1/6.
It has rounded the recurring decimal 0.1666… to fit its display.
Classify 7/20, 5/6, 11/25 and 4/9 as terminating or recurring.
Order 0.4, 0.44, 0.444… and 4/9 on a number line, noting any equality.
Does 6/15 terminate? Simplify the fraction before explaining.
Yes. 6/15 = 2/5 = 0.4. Classification uses the simplified fraction.
Use long division or a calculator to investigate 1/11. State the repeating block and explain why the displayed digits alone are not a proof.
1/11 = 0.090909…; block 09 repeats. Repeating remainders in long division establish continuation beyond the finite screen.
AC9M8N04: 6; work from left to right for multiplication and division.
-4² = -(4²) = -16. (-4)² = 16 because the negative number is the base.
An account starts at -$18, receives $45, then has $62 withdrawn. Find and interpret its balance.
Find -3/4 - 1/2. Explain its position relative to -1.
-5/4 = -1.25, which is one quarter to the left of -1.
A student claims multiplication always increases a number. Give a counterexample using a positive fraction.
For example, 8 × 1/2 = 4. Multiplying a positive number by a factor between zero and one decreases it.
AC9M8N05: A jacket is reduced by 25% from $80. Find its sale price.
72. One eighth of 64 is 8, so add 8.
A student subtracts $20 from $200 for a 20% discount. Correct the calculation.
20% of $200 is $40; the reduced price is $160.
Plan A costs $25 plus $0.10 per text. Plan B costs $40 for unlimited texts. Find the number of texts at equal cost and state when each is cheaper.
150 texts. A is cheaper below 150; B is cheaper above 150, assuming no other charges.
For this fictional pricing example, add a 10% tax after a 30% discount on $120. Find the final amount.
A $100 price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Is it back to $100? Explain the different bases.
No. $100 → $120 → $96. The decrease is calculated on $120.
A model predicts 18.6 packs of tiles are required. Packs are sold whole. What should the purchase model recommend, and what else should be checked?
At least 19 packs. Check the model's area measurements and whether a suitable allowance for cuts or breakages is needed.
AC9M8A01: Factorise 8x + 12 using the greatest common factor.
2a + 12; combine like variable terms and constants separately.
Give two expressions equivalent to 6x + 9 and justify them for every x.
For example, 3(2x + 3) and 2(3x + 4) + 1; expansion gives 6x + 9 in each case.
A rectangle has width 4 and length 2x + 3. Express its area in expanded and factorised forms.
Two expressions give the same result at x = 0. Does that prove equivalence? Use x + 2 and 3x + 2 to explain.
No. Both give 2 at x = 0, but give 3 and 5 at x = 1. An algebraic identity must hold for every permitted value.
AC9M8A02: Points (-2,-3), (-1,-1), (0,1), (1,3), (2,5), joined by a straight line.
Solve x - 4 < 9 and describe its number-line representation.
x < 13; open circle at 13 with values to its left shaded.
A student solves 2x + 5 = 17 as x = 11. Repair the solution and verify it.
(0,4) and (4,0). Set x = 0 and y = 0 respectively.
Solve -2x ≤ 8. Explain what happens when dividing by -2.
x ≥ -4; division by a negative reverses the inequality.
A graph shows y = 3x crossing the horizontal line y = 12 at (4,12). Which equation solution does this show?
3x = 12 has solution x = 4, the x-coordinate of the intersection.
AC9M8A03: A gym charges a $20 joining fee and $8 per week. Write C in terms of weeks w and state the starting cost.
C = 20 + 8w; at w = 0, the cost is $20.
For a printing model C = 5n + 12, find the cost of 10 items and explain 12.
C = $62. The $12 is a fixed setup charge in this model.
A table gives costs 9, 13, 17, 21 for 0, 1, 2, 3 hours. Write a linear rule.
Why is a fixed charge plus a constant hourly charge represented by a straight line?
Equal increases in hours produce equal increases in cost; the fixed charge sets the starting value.
Hire A costs 15 + 4h dollars; B costs 9 + 6h dollars. Find their break-even time and cost.
A poster printer charges $18 setup and $3 per poster. Make a table for 0, 5 and 10 posters, then interpret the graph's intercept.
Costs $18, $33, $48. The vertical intercept is the setup cost. Whole poster counts are appropriate inputs.
For the two hire plans above, which is cheaper for 5 hours? Justify numerically.
A costs $35 and B $39, so A is $4 cheaper.
A hire company rounds any partial hour up to a full hour. Is C = 15 + 4h an exact model for 2.2 actual hours? Explain.
No, not if h means unrounded elapsed hours. The billed hours are 3, so cost is $27; rounding changes the model.
AC9M8A04: Compare y = 2x + 1 with y = 2x + 4. What is unchanged and what changes?
The slope remains 2; every y-value increases by 3, so the graph shifts up 3.
Use graphing software to compare y = -2x + 5 and y = 2x + 5. State a conjecture about the signs of their slopes.
Both cross the y-axis at 5. The negative-slope graph decreases from left to right; the positive-slope graph increases.
Disprove ‘every increasing sequence is linear’ using 1, 4, 9, 16.
Differences are 3, 5, 7, which are not constant, although the values increase.
For n = 1, 2, 3, 4, values are 4, 7, 10, 13. Conjecture a linear rule and test n = 4.
Compare y = 2x + 1 and y = 5x + 1 using x = 0, 1, 2. What changes?
Values are 1,3,5 and 1,6,11. The intercept is unchanged; the second line has a larger slope.
A learner concludes two lines never meet after viewing only -1 ≤ x ≤ 1. What should be checked?
Expand the viewing window or solve for their intersection. A limited graph window does not prove they never meet.
Test the conjecture that y = mx + c passes through (0,c) for m = -3, 0 and 4 with c = 2. Explain why it works generally.
All give y = 2 at x = 0. In general m × 0 + c = c.
AC9M8M01: A 10 m by 6 m rectangle has a 3 m by 2 m rectangular corner removed. Find the remaining area.
Find the perimeter of that L-shape, counting every boundary edge.
32 m. Removing the corner replaces lengths 3 and 2 with equal-length inner edges.
Explain why area is measured in m² and perimeter in m.
Area counts square units covering a surface; perimeter measures one-dimensional boundary length.
A learner adds the cut-out's 6 m² to the rectangle's area. Correct the model.
The cut-out removes material, so subtract its area rather than add it.
Join an 8 m by 5 m rectangle to a 4 m by 3 m rectangle along one complete 3 m edge, with no overlap. Find total area and perimeter.
For the joined shape above, why is the shared edge subtracted twice when adding perimeters?
Both original perimeters count it, but after joining it is an internal edge and contributes nothing to the outside boundary.
A floor is a 6 m by 4 m rectangle plus a 2 m by 3 m rectangular extension, with no overlap. Find carpet area before any waste allowance.
Two composite shapes have equal areas. Must they require equal fencing lengths? Give a numerical counterexample.
No. A 2 m by 6 m rectangle and a 3 m by 4 m rectangle both have area 12 m² but perimeters 16 m and 14 m.
AC9M8M02: Find the volume of a rectangular prism 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm.
Why does length × width alone not give a rectangular prism's volume?
It gives one face's area. Multiply by the perpendicular depth to count the layers of cubic units.
A right triangular prism has triangular cross-sectional area 12 cm² and length 9 cm. Find its volume.
A tank has internal dimensions 60 cm by 30 cm by 40 cm. Find its full capacity.
That tank is filled to a depth of 25 cm. How much water does it contain?
Which holds more: a 0.04 m³ container or a 35 L container? Explain the conversion.
0.04 m³ = 40 L, so it holds 5 L more.
A prism's cross-sectional area is doubled and its length is halved. What happens to volume? Explain.
AC9M8M03: Find the circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm in terms of π.
Find the area of a circle of diameter 10 m.
The radius is 5 m, so area = 25π m².
Explain the difference between circumference and area.
Circumference is boundary length; area is the surface enclosed.
A learner uses 2πr to calculate area. Repair the formula and name the units for r in centimetres.
Use πr², with area in cm². 2πr gives circumference in cm.
A circular pond has radius 4 m. A path of width 1 m surrounds it. Find the path's area.
A wheel has diameter 60 cm. How far does it travel in 10 complete rotations, assuming no slip?
If a radius doubles, compare the new circumference and area with the originals.
Circumference doubles; area becomes four times as large.
Find a circle's radius if its area is 49π cm². Check it in the area formula.
AC9M8M04: Find the duration from 09:35 to 14:20 on the same day.
For this problem, Perth is UTC+8 and Sydney UTC+10. Convert 18:30 Perth time to Sydney time.
20:30 on the same day. The specified Sydney time is 2 hours ahead.
Find the duration from Monday 23:40 to Tuesday 01:15.
1 hour 35 minutes: 20 minutes to midnight and 75 minutes after.
A flight leaves at 22:40 origin time and lasts 2 h 35 min. The destination is 1 hour ahead. Find arrival day and local time.
02:15 the next day at the destination: 01:15 in origin time, then add one hour.
At 00:30 Tuesday in UTC+10, what day and time is it in UTC+8?
Using offsets UTC+10, UTC+8 and UTC+9, compare meetings at 09:00 and 18:00 in UTC+10. Give all local times and a reasoned choice.
09:00 becomes 07:00 and 08:00; 18:00 becomes 16:00 and 17:00. Either justified choice is acceptable; the later option avoids the 07:00 start.
Why should actual travel planning check the date and current local time-zone rules rather than assume a city always uses one offset?
Some places change offsets seasonally. A stated offset is sufficient for these exercises, but real planning needs the applicable date and rule.
AC9M8M05: A runner travels 5 km in 25 minutes. Find average speed in km/h.
Find the price per kilogram if 750 g costs $6.
Compare $4 for 500 g with $7 for 1 kg using unit rates.
$8/kg compared with $7/kg. The 1 kg pack has the lower unit price.
Data plans offer 20 GB for $16, 50 GB for $30, or 100 GB for $45. Compare dollars per GB.
A cyclist rides 18 km in 45 minutes and 12 km in 30 minutes. Find average speed for riding time only.
30 km in 1.25 h gives 24 km/h. Rest time is excluded as requested.
A tap supplies 9 L in 30 seconds at a steady rate. How much in 2 minutes? State the assumption.
36 L, assuming the flow rate remains constant.
A driver averages 60 km/h for one hour and 30 km/h for two hours. Why is the overall average not 45 km/h? Calculate it.
The times are unequal. Total distance 120 km divided by 3 h gives 40 km/h.
AC9M8M06: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find its hypotenuse.
A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 m and one leg 5 m. Find the other leg.
Explain how to identify the hypotenuse before using Pythagoras' theorem.
It is opposite the right angle and is the longest side of a right triangle.
A learner says the hypotenuse of a 3–4 right triangle is 7. Correct the reasoning.
Square the legs before adding: c² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = 5.
A ladder reaches 4 m up a vertical wall and its base is 1.5 m from the wall on level ground. Find its length to two decimal places.
Test whether sides 9, 12 and 15 form a right triangle.
A rectangle is 7 cm wide and 9 cm long. Find its diagonal, giving an exact and approximate answer.
Can Pythagoras' theorem be applied to every triangle by labelling its longest side c? Explain.
No. The triangle must be right-angled. Labelling alone does not establish that condition.
AC9M8M07: Seven parts total, $12 per part: $24 and $60.
A map uses scale 1:50 000. Find the real distance represented by 6 cm.
A learner shares $60 in the ratio 2:3 by dividing by 3. What should the first calculation be?
Divide $60 by 2 + 3 = 5 to find $12 per part, then allocate $24 and $36.
Flour and sugar are mixed in the ratio 5:2. How much sugar goes with 350 g flour?
A 240 km journey uses 7 L of fuel per 100 km. Estimate fuel use and cost at a fictional $2 per litre.
16.8 L and $33.60, assuming the stated consumption rate applies throughout.
A mix uses red and blue paint in ratio 3:2. You add 1 L to each part of a 3 L and 2 L mixture. Is the colour ratio unchanged? Explain.
No. It becomes 4:3, not 3:2. Equivalent ratios require proportional scaling.
Why might actual fuel use differ from the journey model above? Name two relevant factors.
For example, traffic stops, speed, hills, load or driving conditions can alter the consumption rate.
AC9M8SP01: Two triangles have side lengths 5, 7 and 8 cm. Are they congruent? State the condition.
Yes, SSS: all corresponding side lengths match.
Two triangles have equal angles but corresponding side lengths 3 cm and 6 cm. What can be concluded?
They are similar, with scale factor 2 from the smaller to the larger, but not congruent.
A corresponding side changes from 4 cm to 10 cm in similar triangles. Find the scale factor.
Does equal area prove two triangles congruent? Give a counterexample.
No. Right triangles with legs 3 and 4, and 2 and 6, both have area 6 but different side lengths.
Similar triangles have matching sides 6 cm and 15 cm. Another side of the smaller is 8 cm. Find its match.
Two triangles each have sides 5 cm and 7 cm with the included angle 60°. Explain why they are congruent.
SAS: two corresponding sides and the angle between them match.
A triangle is reflected in a line. Which lengths and angles change?
None of the side lengths or angle sizes change; the image is congruent, although its orientation changes.
A learner checks two side ratios for triangle similarity but ignores the third. Why can this be insufficient?
The unchecked side may break proportionality. Use a complete valid condition such as SSS similarity or two matching angles.
AC9M8SP02: State two properties of every parallelogram.
For example, opposite sides are parallel and equal; opposite angles are equal.
Find the fourth angle of a quadrilateral with angles 95°, 80° and 110°.
Explain why a rectangle is a parallelogram.
It has two pairs of parallel opposite sides; its right angles are additional properties.
A rhombus has four equal sides but need not have right angles. A square is a special rhombus.
A parallelogram has one angle of 68°. Find its other three angles.
112°, 68°, 112°; adjacent angles are supplementary and opposite angles equal.
Draw diagonal AC in parallelogram ABCD. Explain how the triangles can establish AB = CD.
Alternate angles at the parallel sides match and AC is shared, giving congruent triangles by ASA; corresponding sides AB and CD are equal.
The diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other. Must they have equal lengths? Use a parallelogram as evidence.
No. A non-rectangular parallelogram can have unequal diagonals that still bisect each other.
What extra condition turns a rhombus into a square? Explain why one right angle is enough.
One right angle suffices: adjacent angles are supplementary and opposite angles equal, so all four become right angles.
AC9M8SP03: Use x for east, y for north and z for up. Write the point 3 east, 2 north and 5 up from the origin.
+3 in x, no change in y, +4 in z.
Why do (2,3,4) and (2,4,3) usually describe different locations?
The y and z values refer to different axes. Swapping them changes northing and height.
A point is (4,1,0). What does its final coordinate tell you?
It is at height zero on the plane z = 0.
List the eight vertices of a box extending 3 units east, 2 north and 4 up from the origin, with edges along the axes.
Start at (2,3,1). Move 4 west, 2 north and 3 up. Find the endpoint.
Use a 3D graphing tool to plot A(1,2,3) and B(1,2,6). Which axis is AB parallel to?
The z-axis; x and y stay constant while z changes.
A plan view hides height. Explain why two points can occupy the same position on the plan but differ in 3D.
They can have equal x and y but different z values, for example (1,2,3) and (1,2,6).
AC9M8SP04: Design a side-length algorithm to test triangle congruence. How should it handle the order of the supplied sides?
Sort each triangle's side lengths, then compare corresponding entries; three matches establish SSS congruence.
After sorting both are (3,4,5), so congruent.
For triangle similarity, compare sorted sides (3,4,5) and (6,8,10). Show every ratio.
An algorithm declares similarity when only the longest-side ratio matches a chosen scale factor. Test (3,4,5) and (3,4,10).
The test is insufficient; the shorter-side ratios are 1 while the longest is 2. Also 3 + 4 < 10, so the second input is not a valid triangle.
Add a check for invalid triangle lengths before testing similarity.
Require all sides positive and the two smaller sides to sum to more than the largest.
Write an if/else step that distinguishes congruent from similar when all three side ratios match.
If the common ratio is 1, classify as congruent; otherwise classify as similar but different in size.
Test the complete algorithm on (2,3,4) and (4,6,8), naming the branch reached.
Both are valid triangles; common scale factor 2 gives similar but not congruent.
Why should an algorithm be tested with a non-example as well as a matching pair?
A non-example checks that the decision rule rejects incorrect cases rather than always returning a positive classification.
AC9M8ST01: A school wants to estimate travel methods for all 600 students by asking 40 students. Identify population and sample.
Population: all 600 students. Sample: the 40 selected students.
The school asks all 600 students. Is this a census or a sample survey?
A census, if information is collected from every member of the population.
Write a neutral question about travel to school with a clear time reference.
For example, ‘What was your main way of travelling to school today?’ with balanced options and another-option response.
Why might surveying only a researcher's friends misrepresent the school?
Friends may share year level, location or habits; students outside that group have no chance of selection.
Describe a random way to select 40 students from the full school roll.
Assign numbers to the full roll and use a random-number tool to choose 40 distinct numbers, handling nonresponse transparently.
Compare this method with asking the first 40 students at the bicycle racks.
The bicycle-rack sample is convenient but likely overrepresents cyclists; a random school-wide sample gives broader selection opportunities.
Would counting cars passing the school be an experiment or an observation? Explain.
Observation: traffic is recorded without deliberately changing a condition.
Suggest an advantage and a practical limitation of a census here.
It can describe all students' responses, but contacting everyone takes time and incomplete responses can still cause problems.
AC9M8ST02: Find mean, median and range for 4, 6, 7, 9, 14.
A sample is 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. Describe the distribution and identify the unusually large value.
Most values cluster at 2–4, with a long right tail caused by 18; right-skewed.
Compare A: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and B: 2, 3, 6, 9, 10 using median and range.
Both medians are 6. Ranges are 4 and 8; B is more spread out.
Why could reporting only the mean be misleading for 2, 3, 3, 4, 18?
Mean 6 is pulled above the cluster by 18. Median 3 and a description of spread/outlier give more context.
A learner records their own class's heights. Is this primary or secondary data for that learner?
Primary data, because the learner collected it directly.
The learner then analyses heights from a published survey. What should be checked before comparing it with the class?
Check measurement units, age group, collection method, date and sampling method so the populations and measurements are comparable.
A school sample selected at sports training has greater median weekly exercise than a random school sample. Give a plausible sampling explanation.
The training sample may overrepresent students who exercise more; the difference need not describe the whole school.
Use software or a dot plot to compare the two five-value sets above. Write a cautious conclusion about their centres and spreads.
Both sample centres are 6, but B is more variable. The small samples alone do not establish a population-wide difference.
AC9M8ST03: Two random samples of 20 students contain 8 and 12 bus users. Find the sample proportions.
Does that difference prove one sample was selected incorrectly? Explain.
No. Random samples from the same population naturally vary.
How does increasing random sample size usually affect variation in sample proportions?
It usually reduces variation between samples, without guaranteeing an exact population proportion.
A simulation gives proportions 0.35, 0.60, 0.45 from samples of 20. Find their range.
For samples of 200, proportions are 0.48, 0.52, 0.49. Compare their range with the previous one.
0.04, or 4 percentage points, which is smaller than 25 percentage points.
Do three trials prove larger samples always lie closer to the population value? Explain.
No. They illustrate a tendency. Any individual random sample can deviate; more repeated trials provide better evidence about typical variation.
Design a digital simulation to compare variation for sample sizes 20 and 200 from a population with 50% successes.
Generate independent 0/1 outcomes with equal chances, repeat many samples at each size, calculate proportions, and compare their distributions using the same display scale.
AC9M8ST04: Form a statistical question about how Year 8 students travel to school that could be investigated with a sample.
For example, ‘What proportion of Year 8 students used active transport to school today?’ Define which methods count as active transport.
Explain why asking only students arriving by bicycle would be a poor sampling plan.
It deliberately overrepresents one transport method and excludes many others.
Describe a fair sample selection from a Year 8 roll of 180 students.
Randomly select, for example, 45 distinct student numbers from the complete roll; report nonresponse rather than silently replacing it with friends.
In the sample, 18 of 45 students use active transport. Estimate the corresponding proportion and number among 180 students.
40%, corresponding to about 72 students if the sample reasonably represents the population.
Why should the estimate be reported as approximate?
Sampling variation and possible nonresponse mean the sample may not exactly match the population.
The next day's sample gives 22 of 45. Does this prove the school's travel habits permanently changed?
No. Sample variation, daily conditions and different respondents could explain the difference.
State two ethical choices for collecting travel information.
Collect only needed information, avoid names or addresses in reports, allow students to decline, and report grouped results.
Write a conclusion using the 18-of-45 result and one limitation.
About 40% of the sampled Year 8 students used active transport that day. The estimate may vary with the day and the sample; it is not an exact count of all students.
AC9M8P01: If P(rain) = 0.3, find P(no rain) for the same specified period.
A bag has 4 red, 3 blue and 5 green counters. Find P(not red) for one random draw.
Is ‘blue’ the complement of ‘red’ in that bag? Explain.
No. ‘Not red’ includes both blue and green.
A fair die is rolled. Find the probability of not rolling a multiple of 3.
Multiples of 3 are 3 and 6, so P(not a multiple) = 4/6 = 2/3.
Why must an event and its complement not overlap?
An outcome cannot both satisfy the event and fail to satisfy it; together they cover the whole sample space.
A game has probability 7/20 of winning and no draws. Find the probability of losing.
If draws become possible, can losing still automatically be called the complement of winning? Explain.
No. The complement of winning includes losing and drawing.
AC9M8P02: List the sample space for two ordered fair coin tosses.
Find the probability of exactly one head.
In 30 students, 12 play chess, 15 play music and 5 do both. Complete the four Venn regions.
Chess only 7; both 5; music only 10; neither 8.
Using that class, find P(chess or music), including those doing both.
Convert the class information to a two-way table with chess/no chess rows and music/no music columns.
Chess row: 5 music, 7 no music. No-chess row: 10 music, 8 no music. Total 30.
A learner adds 12 + 15 and claims 27 students do at least one activity. Explain the error.
The 5 doing both were counted twice; subtract the overlap once to obtain 22.
A shirt has two colour choices and three size choices. List all colour-size combinations using red/blue and S/M/L.
Red-S, Red-M, Red-L, Blue-S, Blue-M, Blue-L; six combinations.
Does listing six combinations make them equally likely purchases? Explain.
No. Listing outcomes alone does not determine their probabilities; customers may prefer some combinations.
AC9M8P03: For two independent fair coin tosses, list the outcomes and find P(two heads).
A simulation produces two heads in 23 of 100 trials. Find relative frequency.
Must a correct 100-trial simulation produce exactly 25 two-head outcomes? Explain.
No. Random variation makes the observed count fluctuate.
Why would reusing the first toss's result as the second toss be an incorrect simulation of independent tosses?
It permits only HH and TT, excluding HT and TH and changing the probabilities.
Describe a digital rule for one valid two-toss trial.
Generate two separate independent random values with equal H/T chances, then record success only if both are H.
A 1000-trial run has 248 successes. Compare its relative frequency with the 100-trial result above.
0.248 is closer to 0.25 than 0.23 is, in these runs.
Does that comparison prove every longer simulation will be closer?
No. More trials generally stabilise relative frequency, but any particular run can vary.
Design a results table for five 100-trial runs. Which columns support a fair comparison?
Run number, total trials, success count, relative frequency and theoretical probability; keep the event definition and simulation rules unchanged.
AC9M9ST04: Choose a display for counts of students' favourite sports and justify it.
A bar chart compares categorical counts; separate bars preserve the categories.
Choose a display to investigate association between height and arm span.
A scatterplot, with one paired point per person and labelled measurement axes.
Choose a display for a town's monthly rainfall over two years when the aim is to see change over time.
A time-series line graph with months in order and rainfall units labelled.
Why is a pie chart unsuitable for showing the relationship between height and arm span?
It shows parts of a whole, not paired values of two numerical variables.
Two bar charts show the same counts, 48 and 52. One axis begins at 0, the other at 47. Explain how appearance changes.
The truncated axis exaggerates the visual difference; a zero baseline is important when bar lengths represent counts.
For travel times 10, 12, 12, 15, 18, 35 minutes, make a dot plot and describe what a mean alone could hide.
Dots at the listed values, with two at 12. Most cluster at 10–18 while 35 is unusually high; the mean obscures that structure.
When comparing two histograms of related data, why should bin widths and axis scales be checked?
Different bin widths or scales can create misleading apparent differences in shape or spread.
A graph is labelled ‘sales’ with no units or time period. Name two repairs needed before interpreting a trend.
Specify whether sales means item count or money, and label the time scale and period. Other relevant missing context may also be identified.
AC9M9ST05: Plan a question investigating whether students who walk to school report longer travel times than those who cycle. Name the data types needed.
Travel mode is categorical; journey time is numerical. Define the school population and a consistent journey/time reference.
Explain why surveying only a cycling club weakens this investigation.
It does not represent both travel groups or the wider student population fairly.
A sample has walking times 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 and cycling times 5, 7, 9, 11, 18. Compare medians and ranges.
Walking median 12, range 8. Cycling median 9, range 13; cyclists have a lower sample median but greater spread.
Do these data prove cycling causes every student to arrive faster? Explain.
No. Small observational samples, differing distances and other variables prevent that causal or universal claim.
Name two contextual variables that would help interpret the travel-time comparison.
For example, distance travelled, route, traffic, age or weather.
A published travel survey includes adults, while the new survey includes Year 9 students. What must a comparison acknowledge?
The populations differ. Collection methods, locations, definitions and dates may also differ.
Write a cautious conclusion from the ten supplied times.
In these samples the cycling median is 3 minutes lower, but times overlap and the samples are small. The result may not generalise.
Suggest one improvement that would strengthen the evidence and explain why.
For example, collect a larger reasonably representative sample and compare similar travel distances; this reduces some sampling or confounding problems.
AC9M10ST04: A group has 40 students: 20 walk to school, 12 play sport, and 8 both walk and play sport. Complete a two-way table.
Walk/sport 8; walk/no sport 12; no walk/sport 4; no walk/no sport 16. Row totals 20,20; column totals 12,28.
What proportion of walkers play sport?
What proportion of non-walkers play sport?
Compare those conditional proportions. What possible relationship do they suggest in this group?
Sport participation is more common among walkers in this group, 40% versus 20%. This suggests association, not causation.
A learner divides 8 by 40 to answer ‘What proportion of walkers play sport?’ Explain the denominator error.
The question restricts the group to 20 walkers. 8/40 instead gives the joint proportion among all students.
If there were 30 walkers and 10 non-walkers, why would raw sport counts alone be a poor comparison?
The group sizes differ; compare within-group proportions to account for the different denominators.
Why does the observed association not prove walking makes students play sport?
Other factors may influence both activities, and this is an observational comparison.
Name a limitation of using this one group to make a claim about all students.
The group is small and may not be representative of the wider student population.
AC9M10ST05: Plan an investigation of the association between a plant's height and leaf count. State the paired variables and an investigable question.
Measure height and count leaves on each plant. For example, ‘Do taller plants in this garden tend to have more leaves?’
Why must height and leaf count be recorded together for each plant rather than as two unrelated lists?
The pairing is needed to investigate how the two measurements vary together.
For fictional pairs (height in cm, leaves): (5,3), (8,5), (11,6), (14,9), (17,10), describe the trend in a scatterplot.
A positive, approximately linear association: taller plants in this sample tend to have more leaves.
Does this prove increased height causes additional leaves? Explain.
No. Age, species or growing conditions may influence both measurements; association alone does not establish causation.
Add the pair (30,2). Explain why it deserves investigation before fitting a trend.
It is far from the main pattern and may strongly influence the fitted relation. Check recording, measurement and whether it belongs to the same population.
Why is predicting leaf count for a 100 cm plant from these data risky?
It is extrapolation far beyond the observed range; the relationship may change.
Suggest a sampling plan and one controlled definition to improve the investigation.
Sample plants reasonably across the intended population; define how height is measured and which leaves are counted. Restrict or record species and age where appropriate.
Write a conclusion that acknowledges both the trend and a limitation.
The initial five plants show a positive association between height and leaf count, but the small sample and possible species or age differences limit generalisation.
